lesson.title: du, Sie & the T–V Line
lesson.subtitle: du ↔ thou, Sie ↔ they — the surviving T–V distinction English retired

hook.title: English Used to Have This Choice
hook.content: English once had two words for 'you': thou (close, informal) and you (distant, respectful). Linguists call it the T–V distinction — from Latin tu and vos. German still runs the full system: du (informal, one person) and Sie (formal, always capitalized). And here is the twist: Sie IS they — formal address borrows the third-person plural, exactly as the royal 'we' borrows the first. Sie sind (you-are-formal) agrees like they are, not like you are. English threw away thou; German kept both words alive — and the choice still matters socially every single day.

footnotes.title: The Quaker Fossil
footnotes.content: English's thou survived longest in Quaker speech — 'thee' and 'thou' as everyday address into the 20th century. German du survived everywhere, and even modern marketing calls its customers du (Du bist Deutschland). The informal pronoun never died on the continent.

pattern.title: The Social Switchboard
pattern.content: du: friends, family, children, pets, God, classmates, colleagues after the offer — one person, informal, verb takes the -st you have drilled (du hast, du bist, du sollst — thou hast, thou art, thou shalt!). Sie: strangers, officials, elders, customers, everyone until offered otherwise — grammatically third-person PLURAL: Sie sind, Sie haben, Sie kommen ('they are/have/come', but meaning you-formal). The switch ritual: the senior or host offers — Wir können du sagen? — and the informal door opens. Dative twins: dir (to-thee, informal) vs Ihnen (to-you-formal, always capital-I).
pattern.linguist_note: The formal Sie is capitalized even in mid-sentence to distinguish it from sie ('she/they'). Dir ↔ thee and Ihnen ↔ ye/you-formal preserve the exact medieval etiquette ladder both languages once ran.

exercises.prompt: Match the T–V forms with their English twins:
exercises.explanation: The T–V ladder: du/dir for the close circle, Sie/Ihnen for the respectful distance — English retired it, German lives in it.

exercises.prompt: Formal agreement check: 'Sie _____ Lehrer.' (You are a teacher — formal):
exercises.meaning: Sie sind Lehrer — formal 'you' agrees like 'they'
exercises.explanation: Sie borrows the third-person PLURAL: Sie sind, never Sie bist. The respect is grammatical distance.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence addresses a friend informally?
exercises.meaning: Du bist lustig = you (thou) are funny
exercises.explanation: du + bist: the informal address — thou art funny, with the -st ending doing its Shakespearean work.

exercises.prompt: What archaic English pronoun is the exact twin of 'du'?
exercises.explanation: TH → D: thou hardened into du. Same word, same ancient informality.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the formal thank-you: 'I thank you (formal)'
exercises.explanation: Ihnen — capital I, formal dative. To a friend you would say Ich danke dir; to a stranger, Herr. The T–V line runs straight through the dative.

summary.outcome: Choose du or Sie correctly and conjugate each with the right agreement.

use_example.german: Ich danke Ihnen. — Ich danke dir.

summary.takeaway: du ↔ thou (informal), Sie ↔ they-as-formal (plural agreement), dir ↔ thee, Ihnen ↔ formal: the T–V line English retired.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Greetings & Goodbyes Gym — the formulas in real dialogue switches.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from du, Sie & the T–V Line (I thank you (formal — to-you-formal)):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich danke Ihnen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of du, Sie & the T–V Line without relying on short-term echo.

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

dir.etymology_derivation: Dative of du — the exact twin of archaic English 'I give it thee'; the dative is the giving case. [wiktionary]

sollen.etymology_derivation: Direct twin of English "shall" and "should" (Shakespeare: "thou shalt" ↔ German "du sollst").

herr.context_translation: The gentleman is called Mr. Müller.
herr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hairaz 'grey' — the grey-haired one, cognate with English hoar. [wiktionary]

blut.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *blōþą — the identical twin of English blood. [wiktionary]

reis.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Late Latin rīsum, Greek órūza — the same trade-route loan as English rice. [wiktionary]

birne.context_phrase: Ich esse eine Birne zum Nachtisch.
birne.context_translation: I eat a pear for dessert.
birne.etymology_derivation: From Vulgar Latin pira, plural of Latin pirum; also the 'bulb' of die Glühbirne. [wiktionary]

joghurt.context_phrase: Zum Frühstück esse ich Joghurt mit Obst.
joghurt.context_translation: For breakfast I eat yogurt with fruit.
joghurt.etymology_derivation: Joghurt — borrowed from Ottoman Turkish yoğurt, exactly like English yogurt; standard German uses der, Austria and Switzerland often das. [wiktionary]

ängstlich.etymology_derivation: From Angst 'fear, dread' + the suffix -lich — literally angst-like, inclined to fear. [wiktionary]

ellbogen.context_phrase: Ich habe mir den Ellbogen gestoßen.
ellbogen.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German elenboge, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô, literally ell plus bow. English elbow is the same compound of the same two roots. [wiktionary]

feder.context_phrase: Die Feder fällt langsam zu Boden.
feder.context_translation: The feather falls slowly to the ground.
feder.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fëdara, from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from PIE *péth₂r-, feather, wing. English feather is the listed cognate, keeping the th where German has d. [wiktionary]

damit.context_phrase: Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich in Berlin arbeiten kann.
damit.context_translation: I am learning German so that I can work in Berlin.
damit.etymology_derivation: Da (there — the th-to-d twin of English there) plus mit (with, twin of with); the page itself compares English therewith. As a conjunction: so that. [wiktionary]

trotzdem.context_phrase: Es war kalt, trotzdem schwammen wir.
trotzdem.context_translation: It was cold, nevertheless we swam.
trotzdem.etymology_derivation: Trotz (defiance, Middle High German truz) plus dem (that — the th-to-d twin of the/that); literally despite that. English nevertheless is unrelated; the B1 value is its sentence-building role. [wiktionary]

niederlande.context_phrase: Wir fahren mit dem Auto in die Niederlande.
niederlande.context_translation: We drive to the Netherlands by car.
niederlande.etymology_derivation: nieder (low) plus Lande — the exact counterpart of English Netherlands; the page glosses nieder as nether, its th to d twin (as in denken and think). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
